Comparing diets across periods, sizes and regions

Source: vignettes/articles/covariates.Rmd
covariates.Rmd

Most diet questions are comparisons: before and after a change in the ecosystem, small and large predators, one region and another. In DietView a comparison starts with a covariate, a column you declare in dv_spec(). This article shows how to build covariates from years and lengths, how to count what each level holds before reading it, how to draw one sunburst per level so the panels can be compared, and how to cross two covariates.

It uses the public ICES stomach data that ship with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see ?ices_diet), restricted to the four predators with the most prey records. The data were not collected to answer any of the comparisons below: the strata are uneven, and part of the article is about seeing that before drawing conclusions.

library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

four <- c("Atlantic cod", "Atlantic mackerel", "European plaice", "Whiting")
dat  <- dat[dat$predator_common %in% four, ]
table(dat$predator_common)
#> 
#>      Atlantic cod Atlantic mackerel   European plaice           Whiting 
#>              2304              1593              1890              1605

1. Build covariates from years and lengths

region, year and quarter are already columns of the data. Two more are built here: a period from the year and a length class from the predator’s length.

Periods

dv_add_period() cuts years into periods. Look at the years first:

table(dat$predator_common, dat$year)
#>                    
#>                     2020 2021 2022 2023 2024
#>   Atlantic cod         0   13  586 1161  544
#>   Atlantic mackerel    0    0 1593    0    0
#>   European plaice      0    0    0    0 1890
#>   Whiting             17    0 1154  434    0

Only cod spans several years. Mackerel were sampled in 2022 only and plaice in 2024 only, so a period comparison is a cod (and partly whiting) question. We compare 2022 with 2023-2024. The obvious call, dv_add_period(year, breaks = c(2021, 2022, 2024)), would put 2021 into the first period with 2022, because the first period includes its lower break. Make the choice explicit instead:

dat$period <- dv_add_period(dat$year, breaks = c(2021.5, 2022, 2024),
                            labels = c("2022", "2023-2024"))
table(dat$year, dat$period, useNA = "ifany")
#>       
#>        2022 2023-2024 <NA>
#>   2020    0         0   17
#>   2021    0         0   13
#>   2022 3333         0    0
#>   2023    0      1595    0
#>   2024    0      2434    0

The 30 records from 2020 and 2021 now have no period (NA). They stay in the data and in every other comparison; they are only left out of the period panels. A year equal to an inner break belongs to the earlier period, so 2022 falls in the first one.

Length classes

dv_size_bins() cuts lengths into bins. Predators differ in size, so give each its own breaks:

sapply(split(dat$length_cm, dat$predator_common), range)
#>      Atlantic cod Atlantic mackerel European plaice Whiting
#> [1,]            6              17.7              11       9
#> [2,]          104              45.2              54      44
breaks <- list(
  "Atlantic cod"      = c(0, 20, 35, 50, 110),
  "Whiting"           = c(0, 20, 30, 50),
  "Atlantic mackerel" = c(15, 30, 35, 50),
  "European plaice"   = c(10, 20, 30, 60)
)
dat$size_bin <- NA_character_
for (p in names(breaks)) {
  i <- dat$predator_common == p
  dat$size_bin[i] <- as.character(dv_size_bins(dat$length_cm[i], breaks[[p]]))
}
table(dat$predator_common, dat$size_bin, useNA = "ifany")
#>                    
#>                     [0, 20) [10, 20) [15, 30) [20, 30) [20, 35) [30, 35)
#>   Atlantic cod          364        0        0        0      964        0
#>   Atlantic mackerel       0        0      602        0        0      414
#>   European plaice         0      359        0      955        0        0
#>   Whiting               503        0        0      855        0        0
#>                    
#>                     [30, 50) [30, 60) [35, 50) [50, 110)
#>   Atlantic cod             0        0      544       432
#>   Atlantic mackerel        0        0      577         0
#>   European plaice          0      576        0         0
#>   Whiting                247        0        0         0

The breaks are a choice you make on biology and state in your methods. Here the cod and whiting breaks bracket the lengths at which these gadoids turn from crustaceans to fish; the mackerel and plaice breaks split the juveniles from the larger adults. Each bin includes its lower edge (right = FALSE), so a 20 cm cod is in [20, 35). Every break vector covers the whole range shown above; a length outside the breaks would get no bin. Check the table for NA before you go on.

Declare them 

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter", "period", "size_bin")
)
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)

2. Count what each level holds

A level is worth reading only if it holds enough stomachs. Count stomachs, not records: records within a stomach are not independent.

n_stom <- function(d, v) {
  tapply(d$stomach_id, list(d$predator_common, d[[v]]),
         function(z) length(unique(z)))
}
d <- prep$data
n_stom(d, "region")
#>                   Baltic Sea North Sea Skagerrak-Kattegat
#> Atlantic cod             198       731                 62
#> Atlantic mackerel         NA       948                100
#> European plaice           38       429                262
#> Whiting                  167       650                 75
n_stom(d, "quarter")
#>                     1    2   3   4
#> Atlantic cod      570   NA  97 324
#> Atlantic mackerel  NA 1048  NA  NA
#> European plaice   168   NA 561  NA
#> Whiting           551   NA 276  65
n_stom(d, "period")
#>                   2022 2023-2024
#> Atlantic cod       223       764
#> Atlantic mackerel 1048        NA
#> European plaice     NA       729
#> Whiting            625       254

dv_summary(prep, by = "region") gives the same counts with the number of records and prey taxa. The empty cells (NA) are combinations that were never sampled: no mackerel from the Baltic, no plaice in quarters 2 or 4. A comparison across a covariate is possible only for the predators that occur in more than one of its levels.

3. One palette for every panel

Build the colors once, from the tree of all records, so that a taxon has the same color in every panel. With several hundred prey taxa, dv_palette() would have to reuse its 20 colors many times; dv_palette_tree() gives one hue per phylum and lighter tints to the taxa below it:

tree_all <- dv_tree(prep)
pal <- dv_palette_tree(tree_all)
length(pal)
#> [1] 653

The palette is keyed by node, so it works for any tree built from a subset of these records.

4. Cod in 2022 and in 2023-2024 

cod <- d[d$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]

t22 <- dv_build_tree(cod[cod$period %in% "2022", ], prep$ranks,
                     weight_col = spec$weight)
t34 <- dv_build_tree(cod[cod$period %in% "2023-2024", ], prep$ranks,
                     weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(t22, mode = "weight", colors = pal, title = "Atlantic cod, 2022",
            subtitle = "share of prey weight")
dv_sunburst(t34, mode = "weight", colors = pal, title = "Atlantic cod, 2023-2024",
            subtitle = "share of prey weight")

How to read two panels side by side: both start at the same angle and list taxa in the same order, so you read them in the same direction. A taxon does not always sit at the same angle, though. If it is absent from one period, every wedge after it moves round to close the gap. Use color, not position, to find a taxon in both panels, and the hover labels to read its share.

To compare numbers rather than pictures, put the two rank tables side by side. Each column is a share of that period’s records (or weight), unidentified records included, so each column adds up to 100:

side_by_side <- function(ta, tb, names, rank = "Class") {
  a <- dv_rank_table(ta, rank)
  b <- dv_rank_table(tb, rank)
  a <- a[a$label != "NA", c("label", "pct_occ", "pct_w")]
  b <- b[b$label != "NA", c("label", "pct_occ", "pct_w")]
  m <- merge(a, b, by = "label", all = TRUE, suffixes = paste0("_", names))
  m[is.na(m)] <- 0
  m[, -1] <- round(m[, -1], 1)
  m[order(-m[[2]]), ][1:5, ]
}
side_by_side(t22, t34, c("2022", "2023_24"))
#>          label pct_occ_2022 pct_w_2022 pct_occ_2023_24 pct_w_2023_24
#> 5 Malacostraca         57.7       68.6            38.4          18.1
#> 9    Teleostei         19.5       22.4            29.6          73.2
#> 8   Polychaeta          8.2        4.4             5.6           3.7
#> 7  Ophiuroidea          4.8        1.9             1.3           0.1
#> 1     Bivalvia          2.0        0.1             1.0           0.1

By weight, crustaceans fall from 68.6% of the cod diet in 2022 to 18.1% in 2023-2024, and fish rise from 22.4% to 73.2%. Before calling this a change in time, look at what else differs between the two periods:

n_stom(cod, "period")
#>              2022 2023-2024
#> Atlantic cod  223       764
tapply(cod$stomach_id, list(cod$region, cod$period), function(z) length(unique(z)))
#>                    2022 2023-2024
#> Baltic Sea           NA       198
#> North Sea           223       504
#> Skagerrak-Kattegat   NA        62
tapply(cod$stomach_id, list(cod$size_bin, cod$period), function(z) length(unique(z)))
#>           2022 2023-2024
#> [0, 20)     89       119
#> [20, 35)    73       375
#> [35, 50)    43       171
#> [50, 110)   18        99

All the 2022 cod come from the North Sea, while 2023-2024 adds the Baltic and the Skagerrak-Kattegat; and the 2022 sample has proportionally more small cod. The two periods differ in region and in predator size as much as in time, so the difference in the panels cannot be attributed to the period alone. This is the usual situation with survey data assembled after the fact: read the sampling design off the counts before you read the diet off the panels.

5. Cod by length class and by region

Length gives a cleaner contrast, because it varies within every region and period. A small helper puts the stomach count next to the share of fish (Teleostei) in each level:

fish_by <- function(x, v) {
  trees <- lapply(split(x, x[[v]]), function(s)
    dv_build_tree(s, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight))
  out <- t(sapply(trees, function(t) {
    r <- dv_rank_table(t, "Class")
    c(fish_records_pct = round(sum(r$pct_occ[r$label == "Teleostei"]), 1),
      fish_weight_pct  = round(sum(r$pct_w[r$label == "Teleostei"]), 1))
  }))
  cbind(stomachs = n_stom(x, v)[1, rownames(out)], out)
}
by_size <- lapply(split(cod, cod$size_bin), function(x)
  dv_build_tree(x, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight))

fish_share <- fish_by(cod, "size_bin")
fish_share
#>           stomachs fish_records_pct fish_weight_pct
#> [0, 20)        208             14.0            16.3
#> [20, 35)       450             18.8            31.5
#> [35, 50)       215             32.2            56.6
#> [50, 110)      118             50.2            79.7

The share of fish in the cod diet rises steadily with cod length, from 16.3% of the prey weight below 20 cm to 79.7% above 50 cm. The two ends of the size range, with the same palette:

dv_sunburst(by_size[["[0, 20)"]], mode = "weight", colors = pal,
            title = "Atlantic cod, under 20 cm", subtitle = "share of prey weight")
dv_sunburst(by_size[["[50, 110)"]], mode = "weight", colors = pal,
            title = "Atlantic cod, 50 cm and over", subtitle = "share of prey weight")

The same lines work for any of the four predators; only the breaks differ.

By region:

fish_by(cod, "region")
#>                    stomachs fish_records_pct fish_weight_pct
#> Baltic Sea              198             25.8            71.5
#> North Sea               731             27.4            68.8
#> Skagerrak-Kattegat       62             26.7            61.8

At class level the regions are close. Fish make up 71.5% of the cod prey weight in the Baltic Sea, 68.8% in the North Sea and 61.8% in the Skagerrak-Kattegat, where only 62 stomachs were sampled, all in one year. Region, like period, is entangled with the other covariates: the Baltic and Skagerrak-Kattegat cod were all caught in 2023-2024, and their length distributions differ from the North Sea one. A table of stomachs by region and length class (n_stom() on a crossed variable, or the crossed panels below) is the first thing to look at before interpreting any of these differences.

6. Crossing two covariates

Often the question is one covariate within another: does the diet of large cod differ between periods in the same way as that of small ones? First count what each combination holds:

cells <- tapply(cod$stomach_id, list(cod$size_bin, cod$period),
                function(z) length(unique(z)))
cells
#>           2022 2023-2024
#> [0, 20)     89       119
#> [20, 35)    73       375
#> [35, 50)    43       171
#> [50, 110)   18        99

Crossing divides the sample quickly. With 2291 cod records split into eight cells, the largest cod of 2022 come from only 18 stomachs. Decide in advance how many stomachs a cell needs before you interpret it, and report that number with the figure. With a minimum of 30 stomachs, for example, the cells to read are:

which(cells >= 30, arr.ind = TRUE)
#>           row col
#> [0, 20)     1   1
#> [20, 35)    2   1
#> [35, 50)    3   1
#> [0, 20)     1   2
#> [20, 35)    2   2
#> [35, 50)    3   2
#> [50, 110)   4   2

Draw a cell only when it passes:

sub <- cod[cod$size_bin == "[20, 35)" & cod$period %in% "2023-2024", ]
tc  <- dv_build_tree(sub, prep$ranks, weight_col = spec$weight)
dv_sunburst(tc, mode = "occurrence", colors = pal,
            title = "Atlantic cod, 20-35 cm, 2023-2024",
            subtitle = paste(length(unique(sub$stomach_id)), "stomachs; share of prey records"))

The Shiny app does the same interactively: choose a covariate under Facet by covariate and a second one under Cross with, and it draws one panel per combination (run_dietview(prep)).

7. A missing level is not an unidentified prey

Two kinds of NA appear in this article, and they mean different things.

A covariate NA is a record that belongs to no level of the covariate: here the 30 records from 2020 and 2021, which have no period. They are not in any period panel. The dashboard leaves such records out of that covariate’s row of panels, and the Shiny app shows them in a separate “NA” panel, so you can see what was set aside.

A taxonomic NA is a prey record not identified to a rank: a white wedge inside every panel, kept so that each ring still adds up to 100%. It has nothing to do with the covariates:

c(period_na_records    = sum(is.na(d$period)),
  class_na_records_cod = sum(is.na(cod$class)))
#>    period_na_records class_na_records_cod 
#>                   30                  424

Report the first as a sample size (“13 cod records from 2021 were not assigned a period”) and the second as an identification share (“18.4% of the cod prey records were not identified to class”).

8. All strata in one file

dv_build_html() writes every comparison into one HTML file: strata gives each covariate its own row of sunbursts, and cross adds crossed rows. cross = list(c(inner, outer)) reads “inner within outer”: one row per level of outer, one sunburst per level of inner in that row.

dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "ices_by_strata.html"),
              strata = c("region", "quarter", "period", "size_bin"),
              cross  = list(c("size_bin", "period"),    # length classes within periods
                            c("size_bin", "region")),   # length classes within regions
              length_col = "length_cm")

The dashboard draws every cell that holds records, whatever its size, and shows the number of stomachs in each. The small-cell rule is yours to apply when you read it. By default the build stays offline; see the species-cards article for predator photos from iNaturalist, with their authors and licenses.
